summary: Provides alternative ASN.1 modules for the Evidence Record Syntax and its use in the Server-based Certificate Validation Protocol. The new modules use the 2002 version of ASN.1 and follow the conventions of RFC 5911, RFC 5912, and RFC 6268. Nothing changes on the wire, only the syntax description. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The same message is written in a newer spelling style. The message itself is exactly the same.

subtitle: Updated syntax modules for long-term evidence records using modern ASN.1.

tldr.problem: The Evidence Record Syntax (ERS) and its integration with SCVP were originally written using the outdated 1988 version of ASN.1 notation, and developers prefer the newer 2002 version.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides alternative ASN.1 modules for ERS and SCVP-over-ERS using the 2002 ASN.1 syntax, following the conventions of RFCs 5911, 5912, and 6268. The bits on the wire are unchanged.
tldr.outcome: Developers and standards tools can work with modern ASN.1 while maintaining full compatibility with existing implementations.

today: RFC 9169 is an Informational RFC published in December 2021. The original 1988 ASN.1 modules in RFC 4998 and RFC 5276 remain normative, while these new 2002 modules provide an alternative for developers who prefer modern notation.

sections.title: ASN.1 Syntax Update
sections.content:
ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) is a standard way to describe data structures in network protocols. Two versions are widely used: the old 1988 version and the newer 2002 version. Both versions produce the same bits on the wire when encoded, but the 2002 version has cleaner syntax and is actively maintained by ITU-T.

The Evidence Record Syntax (RFC 4998) and its integration with the Server-based Certificate Validation Protocol (SCVP, RFC 5055 and RFC 5276) were originally specified using the 1988 ASN.1 version. This RFC provides modern 2002 ASN.1 modules for both, following the conventions of RFCs 5911, 5912, and 6268.
sections.eli5: ASN.1 is a language for writing down what data looks like. There's an old version and a new version of the language. This note translates old ASN.1 into new ASN.1. Same information, newer language.

sections.title: Evidence Records and SCVP
sections.content:
An Evidence Record is a cryptographic evidence structure that proves documents or data existed at a specific point in time and have not been altered. It uses hash chains and timestamps to create a long-term proof that survives even if the underlying cryptographic algorithms become weak.

The Server-based Certificate Validation Protocol (SCVP) is a protocol for asking a trusted server to validate a certificate. RFC 5276 specifies how to convey Evidence Records within SCVP responses, allowing clients to obtain long-term validation evidence from a server.

The EvidenceRecord structure contains a version, digest algorithms, optional crypto information, optional encryption information, and a sequence of archive timestamps. Each archive timestamp contains a digest algorithm, attributes, optional reduced hash trees, and a timestamp in CMS format.
sections.eli5: An Evidence Record is like a notarized document that says 'this data existed and was unchanged on this date.' SCVP is a protocol for asking a server 'is this certificate real?' The new note lets both use modern ASN.1.

sections.title: The New ASN.1 Modules
sections.content:
The RFC provides two alternative ASN.1 modules.

For RFC 4998 (ERS): The new ERS-2021 module defines the EvidenceRecord structure and related types. It imports AlgorithmIdentifier, digest algorithms, and attributes from the standard modules in RFC 5912 and RFC 6268. The EvidenceRecord consists of a version field, a sequence of digest algorithms, optional cryptographic information, optional encryption information, and a sequence of archive timestamp chains. Each ArchiveTimeStamp contains an optional digest algorithm, optional attributes, optional reduced hash trees, and a ContentInfo (timestamp).

For RFC 5276 (SCVP extensions): The new LTANS-SCVP-EXTENSION-2021 module defines want-backs for evidence records. It imports the SCVP framework and the EvidenceRecord from the ERS module. The module defines EvidenceRecordWantBack structures, which associate an SCVP want-back identifier with an optional EvidenceRecord, and defines six new want-backs for evidence records in SCVP responses.
sections.eli5: The modules define what an Evidence Record looks like and how it fits into SCVP. The new syntax says the same thing as the old syntax, just in cleaner language.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
These new ASN.1 modules produce exactly the same bits on the wire as the original 1988 ASN.1 versions. When encoded using the DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules) or other encoding rules, the byte sequence is identical. This means:

Existing implementations continue to work: Systems that already handle Evidence Records and SCVP will accept and produce the same formats regardless of which ASN.1 module was used to generate them.

Tools and developers benefit: New implementations can use the cleaner 2002 ASN.1 syntax, and standards tools that prefer the newer notation can work with these modules.

Old modules remain normative: The original 1988 ASN.1 modules in RFC 4998 and RFC 5276 are still the authoritative definitions. These new modules are informative, provided as a convenience for developers.
sections.eli5: The same exact message comes out of your computer whether you use the old or new ASN.1 rules. Old systems and new systems understand each other perfectly.

items.title: 1988 ASN.1
items.text: Deprecated, no longer maintained by ITU-T, used in older RFCs

items.title: 2002 ASN.1
items.text: Modern, actively maintained, cleaner syntax, used in recent standards
